summary: This OAuth app lets your Composio-based agent connect to GitHub accounts and act on their repositories. The biggest factor in effort is that each company's GitHub organization can block third-party OAuth apps by default, so private org repos stay hidden until that company's owner approves your app.

verdict.headline: GitHub OAuth apps are self-serve: anyone with a GitHub account can register one for free with no review, but each company's org owner may need to approve it before the agent can see private org repos.
verdict.timeToFirstConnection: About 15 to 30 minutes after you have a GitHub login (estimate, not measured).
verdict.timeToProduction: Same day for personal and public repos. Private repos in each customer org depend on that org owner's approval, which has no predictable timeline.
verdict.activeEffort: About 1 to 2 hours of hands-on work, plus per-customer org approvals.
verdict.approvalWait: None from GitHub for OAuth apps. Per-company org owner approval has no measured wait time.

composio.guidance: Composio has a managed GitHub OAuth app, so you can build and test on it today. Switch to your own GitHub OAuth app before production if you need your own branding on the consent screen, your own scopes, or your own rate limits. Approvals are tied to the app ID, so customers who approved Composio's app will need to approve yours too.

prerequisites.item: A GitHub account that will own the OAuth app (personal, or an organization where you are an admin)
prerequisites.why: Registration requires a GitHub login, and the app is owned by the account you register it under.

prerequisites.item: Access to your Composio dashboard, to create a custom GitHub auth config
prerequisites.why: You need to paste your Client ID and client secret into Composio, and copy the exact callback URL from there.

prerequisites.item: A decision on whether to use an organization as the owner
prerequisites.why: An org gives shared ownership, and it is the path to publisher verification if you ever need it. It is not required to connect.

stages.title: Register the OAuth app on GitHub
stages.goal: You have a GitHub OAuth app with a Client ID and client secret, and a callback URL that matches your Composio config.

steps.text: Sign in to GitHub with the account that will own the app.
steps.detail: Visiting the registration page without a login sends you to the login page. Choose a personal account, or an organization where you are an admin.

steps.text: Open Settings → Developer settings → OAuth apps → New OAuth App.
Fill in the app name, homepage URL, and optional description.
steps.detail: An agent can draft the name, description, and homepage text. You enter them into the form. Use a name that matches your product, since it appears on the consent screen.

Copy the exact callback URL from your Composio custom auth config. The dossier gives https://backend.composio.dev/api/v3.1/toolkits/auth/callback as the v3.1 value, but older docs show /api/v3/. Use whatever your dashboard shows. GitHub matches the callback exactly, so there can be no differences in scheme, host, path, or trailing slash. You can register up to 10 callback URLs.

steps.text: Decide whether to leave "Expire user access tokens" on.
steps.detail: It is on by default for new apps. Leave it on only if your setup handles refresh tokens, which means keeping the refresh token and renewing the access token. The default produces 8-hour access tokens.

steps.text: Click Register, then copy the Client ID and generate a client secret.
steps.detail: Store the secret in your secret manager. Do not commit it to source control.

stages.title: Connect the OAuth app to Composio
stages.goal: A Composio custom GitHub auth config uses your Client ID and secret, and the scopes are reviewed.

steps.text: Create a custom GitHub auth config in the Composio dashboard and paste in the Client ID and client secret.
steps.detail: Check whether the form accepts a GitHub App client ID as well. Composio's custom flow may be built on OAuth apps, so do not assume it works with a GitHub App.

steps.text: Verify that the callback URL in Composio exactly matches the one you registered on GitHub.
steps.detail: An agent can compare the two values and flag differences. A mismatch is the most common setup error.

steps.text: Choose the minimum set of scopes you need.
steps.detail: An agent can draft the scope list from your use case. Include offline_access if you want a refresh token even when expiring tokens are off. Leave out delete_repo unless you need it. Note that repo grants read/write across public, internal, and private repos.

stages.title: Test with your own account and an org
stages.goal: You have connected your personal account and at least one org account, and you know what an unapproved org looks like.

steps.text: Connect your own GitHub account through Composio.
steps.detail: This is the first connection and should take about 15 to 30 minutes including setup.

steps.text: Confirm that personal and public repos are visible.
Connect an account in an organization that has OAuth app restrictions on.
steps.detail: Expect the connection to succeed, but private org repos may be missing or the access request may be pending until an owner approves. Confirm this on a real org before you promise it to customers.

GitHub keeps at most 10 tokens per user, app, and scope, and an app can create at most 10 tokens per hour. A new token beyond the limit revokes an older one, which can break a session your agent is still using.

stages.title: Get customer org approvals and ship
stages.goal: Customers can connect, and their org owners have approved your app where needed.
stages.duration: 30 min + per-company owner approvals (no predictable wait)

steps.text: Give each customer org owner a short approval request.
steps.detail: An agent can draft the request. Owners must approve it themselves in their org settings. Owners can also limit who is allowed to request OAuth app access.

steps.text: Do not ask owners to disable restrictions for the whole org unless they choose to.
steps.detail: Disabling restrictions makes every member's OAuth approvals reach org resources. Owners can do this, but it is their decision.

steps.text: Make sure your code handles token expiry and refresh.
steps.detail: An agent can review your token-refresh path. Access tokens last 8 hours. Refresh tokens expire after 6 months if unused. Older apps may still issue non-expiring tokens.

steps.text: Skip the GitHub Marketplace listing unless you need it.
steps.detail: A Marketplace listing needs a developer agreement, publisher contact details, a privacy-policy link, and a pricing plan. Paid plans and the verified badge require publisher verification. Neither is needed to connect.

scopes.note: Full read/write to public, internal, and private repos, plus org projects, invitations, team memberships, and webhooks. It is the only way to read code in private repos with OAuth apps. Expect broad permissions and say so in your consent copy.
Issues a refresh token for that sign-in even if expiring tokens are off. GitHub Enterprise Server may ignore it.
Destructive. Leave it out unless the agent must delete repos.
Write access to packages. Include only if needed.
Access to security events. Include only if needed.
Used in the probe only. Not described in the dossier, so confirm its meaning on the scopes page before requesting it.

blockers.title: Private org repos are missing after a successful connect
blockers.symptom: The connection succeeds, but the agent sees only personal or public repos. The org may show a pending access request, or the org owner may not have approved the app.
blockers.workaround: Ask the org owner to approve the app in their org's OAuth app settings. If the owner has enabled access restrictions, that is the expected behavior until they approve.

blockers.title: Callback URL mismatch
blockers.symptom: Authorization fails at the callback. The exact GitHub error was not observed, because the probe only reached the login page.
blockers.workaround: Copy the callback URL from the Composio auth config exactly, including scheme, host, path, and trailing slash. Update the GitHub app's callback to match, then retry.

blockers.title: Access token expires after 8 hours
blockers.symptom: API calls start failing with an invalid token error after about 8 hours if your app does not refresh tokens.
blockers.workaround: Refresh the token using the refresh token, or turn off Expire user access tokens if you have a deliberate reason. Confirm which option your Composio flow handles.

blockers.title: Refresh token expires from disuse
blockers.symptom: A user who has not used the connection for about 6 months must reconnect.
blockers.workaround: Prompt the user to reconnect when a refresh fails.

blockers.title: Repeated reconnects revoke older tokens
blockers.symptom: A session that was working stops working after a reconnect, because GitHub revoked an older token.
blockers.workaround: Reuse existing tokens, avoid repeated reconnects, and keep one token per user, app, and scope in the agent's store.

blockers.title: Switching from Composio's app to your own resets approvals
blockers.symptom: Customer orgs that approved Composio's app show private repos as unavailable after you switch to your own app.
blockers.workaround: Plan a re-approval request for each customer org, and send it before the switch.

nuances.text: GitHub recommends GitHub Apps over OAuth apps for fine-grained permissions, user-selected repos, and short-lived tokens. OAuth apps are still a valid choice for this integration, but repo access is coarse.
Registration has no review step and no required business, payment, privacy policy, or demo. This is an inference from the registration docs, not an explicit GitHub statement.
Wildcard callback matching is available but GitHub warns it is a security risk. Keep callbacks exact.
GitHub supports PKCE with S256 only and does not support the implicit flow.
Older GitHub OAuth apps may still default to non-expiring tokens. Check the setting on the app you actually use.
Scopes only limit a token. They never grant more access than the user already has.

agentCanDo: Draft the app name, description, homepage text, and org approval request.
Generate and explain the minimum scope list.
Compare the Composio callback URL with the GitHub callback URL and flag mismatches.
Review the token refresh path in code for 8-hour expiry handling.
Draft the publisher-verification or Marketplace checklist, if you decide to pursue it.
youMustDo: Sign in to GitHub and register the app under your account or org.
Enter the Client ID and client secret into Composio, and generate the secret yourself.
Decide whether to leave Expire user access tokens on.
Connect and test with your own account and a restricted org.
Ask each customer's org owner to approve the app. Owners decide whether to disable restrictions.
Decide whether to pursue Marketplace listing or publisher verification.
